**Operation Torch** (8–16 November 1942) was an [Allied](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allies_of_World_War_II "Allies of World War II") invasion of [French North Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_North_Africa "French North Africa") during [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"). Torch was a compromise operation that met the British objective of securing victory in North Africa while allowing American armed forces the opportunity to begin their fight against [Nazi Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_Germany "Nazi Germany") and [Fascist Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fascist_Italy "Fascist Italy") on a limited scale.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWillmott1984213-2)

The French colonies were aligned with Germany via [Vichy France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vichy_France "Vichy France") but the loyalties of the population were mixed. Reports indicated that they might support the Allies. The American General [Dwight D. Eisenhower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dwight_D._Eisenhower "Dwight D. Eisenhower"), supreme commander of the Allied forces in [Mediterranean theater of the war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mediterranean_and_Middle_East_theatre_of_World_War_II "Mediterranean and Middle East theatre of World War II"), approved plans for a three-pronged attack on [Casablanca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casablanca "Casablanca") (Western), [Oran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oran "Oran") (Centre) and [Algiers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algiers "Algiers") (Eastern), then a rapid move on [Tunis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tunis "Tunis") to catch Axis forces in North Africa from the west in conjunction with the British advance from [Egypt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egypt "Egypt").

The Western Task Force encountered unexpected resistance and bad weather but Casablanca, the principal French Atlantic naval base, was captured after a short siege. The Centre Task Force suffered some damage to its ships when trying to land in shallow water; Oran surrendered after bombardment by British battleships. The Eastern Task Force met less opposition and were able to push inland and compel surrender on the first day.

The success of Torch caused Admiral [François Darlan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Darlan "François Darlan"), commander of the Vichy French forces, who was in Algiers, to order co-operation with the Allies, in return for being installed as [High Commissioner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Civil_and_Military_High_Command "French Civil and Military High Command"), with many other Vichy officials keeping their jobs. Darlan was assassinated by a monarchist six weeks later and the [Free French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_French "Free French") gradually came to dominate the government.

## Background

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Operation_Torch&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")]

### Allied strategy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Operation_Torch&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Allied strategy")]

When the United States entered the Second World War on December 7, 1941, British and Americans met at the [Arcadia Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arcadia_Conference "Arcadia Conference") in Washington D.C. to discuss future strategy. The principle of [Europe first](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europe_first "Europe first") (Germany first) was agreed upon, but British and Americans had different views on how to implement it. Americans favoured a direct approach with first a limited landing in Europe in 1942 ([Operation Sledgehammer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Sledgehammer "Operation Sledgehammer")), and then a follow-up main thrust in 1943 ([Operation Roundup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Roundup_(1942) "Operation Roundup (1942)")). The British pressed for a less ambitious plan. They realized the build-up of American forces ([Operation Bolero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Bolero "Operation Bolero")) would take time, and there was not enough shipping available for large operations. [Winston Churchill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winston_Churchill "Winston Churchill") proposed to invade North Africa.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPack197817%E2%80%9322-3) The head of the [United States Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army "United States Army"), General [George Marshall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Marshall "George Marshall") and the head of the US Navy, [Admiral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Navy "United States Navy")[Ernest King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernest_King "Ernest King") strongly opposed that plan, and were inclined to abandon the Germany first strategy if Churchill persisted. But President [Franklin D. Roosevelt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin_D._Roosevelt "Franklin D. Roosevelt") wanted to support the Soviets and as any Pacific operation would be of no help to them, he agreed to the North-African operation.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPack197817%E2%80%9322-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMackenzie201454%E2%80%9355-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHusen19991270-5) On 14 August 1942 Lt. General [Dwight D. Eisenhower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dwight_D._Eisenhower "Dwight D. Eisenhower") was appointed as Commander in Chief Allied expeditionary Force, and he set up his headquarters in London.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorison1947180-6)

Planners identified Oran, Algiers and Casablanca as key targets. Ideally there would also be a landing at Tunis to secure Tunisia and facilitate the rapid interdiction of supplies travelling via Tripoli to [Erwin Rommel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erwin_Rommel "Erwin Rommel")'s [Afrika Korps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afrika_Korps "Afrika Korps") forces in [Italian Libya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_Libya "Italian Libya"). A compromise would be to land at [Bône](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C3%B4ne "Bône") in eastern Algeria, some 300 miles (480 km) closer to Tunis than Algiers. Limited resources dictated that the Allies could only make three landings and Eisenhower, who believed that any plan must include landings at Oran and Algiers, had two main options: either the western option, to land at Casablanca, Oran and Algiers and then make as rapid a move as possible to Tunis some 500 miles (800 km) east of Algiers once the Vichy opposition was suppressed; or the eastern option, to land at Oran, Algiers and Bône and then advance overland to Casablanca some 500 miles (800 km) west of Oran. He favoured the eastern option because of the advantages it gave to an early capture of Tunis and also because the Atlantic swells off Casablanca presented considerably greater risks to an amphibious landing there than would be encountered in the Mediterranean. The Combined Chiefs of Staff, however, were concerned that should Operation Torch precipitate [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain_during_World_War_II "Spain during World War II") to abandon neutrality and join the Axis, the Straits of Gibraltar could be closed cutting the entire Allied force's lines of communication. They therefore chose the Casablanca option as the less risky since the forces in Algeria and Tunisia could be supplied overland from Casablanca in the event of closure of the straits.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEisenhower194888%E2%80%9389-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacCloskey197136%E2%80%9341-8)

The Morocco landings ruled out the early occupation of Tunisia. But with [British forces advancing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Battle_of_El_Alamein "Second Battle of El Alamein") from Egypt, this would allow the Allies to carry out a [pincer operation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pincer_movement "Pincer movement") against Axis forces in North Africa by mid-January 1943.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacCloskey197141-9)

### Intrigues with Vichy commanders

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Operation_Torch&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Intrigues with Vichy commanders")]

Further information: [Operation Kingpin (World War II)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Kingpin_(World_War_II) "Operation Kingpin (World War II)") and [Henri Giraud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_Giraud "Henri Giraud")

The Allies believed that the Vichy French [Armistice Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armistice_Army "Armistice Army") would not fight, partly because of information supplied by the American [Consul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consul_(representative) "Consul (representative)")[Robert Daniel Murphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Daniel_Murphy "Robert Daniel Murphy") in [Algiers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algiers "Algiers"). The French were former members of the Allies, and US troops were instructed not to fire unless they were fired upon.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPlayfairMolonyFlynnGleave2004126,_141%E2%80%9342-10) The [Vichy French Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vichy_French_Navy "Vichy French Navy") were expected to be very hostile after the British [Attack on Mers-el-Kébir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attack_on_Mers-el-K%C3%A9bir "Attack on Mers-el-Kébir") in June 1940, and the [Syria–Lebanon campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syria%E2%80%93Lebanon_campaign "Syria–Lebanon campaign") in 1941.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPack197856-11)

Allied military strategists needed to consider the political situation in North Africa. The Americans had recognised [Pétain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%A9tain "Pétain") and the Vichy government in 1940, whereas the British did not and had recognised General [Charles de Gaulle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_de_Gaulle "Charles de Gaulle")'s [French National Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_National_Committee "French National Committee") as a government-in-exile instead.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWest_Point-12) After his backing of British operations against the Vichy French in [Dakar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dakar "Dakar") and Syria, de Gaulle did not have many supporters in North Africa.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGelb199265-13) Hence the Allies decided to keep de Gaulle and his [Free French Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_French_Forces "Free French Forces") entirely out of the operation.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacCloskey197135-14)

To gauge the feeling of the Vichy French forces, Murphy was appointed to the American consulate in Algeria. His covert mission was to determine the mood of the French forces and to make contact with elements that might support an Allied invasion. He succeeded in contacting several French officers, including [General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General "General")[Charles Mast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mast "Charles Mast"), the French commander-in-chief in Algiers. These officers were willing to support the Allies but asked for a clandestine conference with a senior Allied general in Algeria.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWest_Point-12) Major General [Mark W. Clark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_W._Clark "Mark W. Clark"), one of Eisenhower's senior commanders, was secretly dispatched to [Cherchell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cherchell "Cherchell") in Algeria aboard the British submarine [HMS _Seraph_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Seraph_(P219) "HMS Seraph (P219)") and met with these Vichy French officers on 21 October 1942. Due to the need to maintain secrecy, the French officers were left in the dark about concrete plans, but they gave Clark detailed information about the military situation in Algiers. These officers also asked French General [Henri Giraud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_Giraud "Henri Giraud") be moved out of Vichy France to take the lead of the operation.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGelb1992157%E2%80%93165-15)

Eventually the Allies [succeeded in slipping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Kingpin_(World_War_II) "Operation Kingpin (World War II)") Giraud out of Vichy France on HMS _Seraph_ to Gibraltar, where Eisenhower had his headquarters, intending to offer him the post of commander in chief of French forces in North Africa after the invasion. However, Giraud would take no position lower than commander in chief of all the invading forces.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGroom2006354-16) When he was refused, he decided to remain "a spectator in this affair".[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAtkinson200266-17)

## Forces

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Operation_Torch&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Forces")]

### Allied forces

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Operation_Torch&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Allied forces")]

Further information: [Operation Torch order of battle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch_order_of_battle "Operation Torch order of battle")

[![Image 21](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/04/Operation_Torch.jpg/250px-Operation_Torch.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Operation_Torch.jpg)

Allied convoys heading from the British Isles to North Africa

The Allies organised three amphibious task forces to simultaneously seize the key ports and airports in Morocco and Algeria, targeting [Casablanca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casablanca "Casablanca"), [Oran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oran "Oran") and Algiers.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGelb1992121-125-18)

A Western Task Force (aimed at Casablanca) was composed of American units, with [Major General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Major_general_(United_States) "Major general (United States)")[George S. Patton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_S._Patton "George S. Patton") in command and [Rear Admiral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rear_Admiral "Rear Admiral")[Henry Kent Hewitt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Kent_Hewitt "Henry Kent Hewitt") heading the naval operations. This Western Task Force consisted of the U.S. [3rd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3rd_Infantry_Division_(United_States) "3rd Infantry Division (United States)") and [9th Infantry Divisions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/9th_Infantry_Division_(United_States) "9th Infantry Division (United States)"), and two battalions from the [U.S. 2nd Armored Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2nd_Armored_Division_(United_States) "2nd Armored Division (United States)"), 35,000 troops in a convoy of over 100 ships. They were transported directly from the United States in the first of a new series of [UG convoys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UG_convoys "UG convoys") providing logistic support for the North African campaign.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHague2000179%E2%80%9380-19)

The Centre Task Force, aimed at Oran, included the U.S. 2nd Battalion [509th Parachute Infantry Regiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/509th_Infantry_Regiment_(United_States) "509th Infantry Regiment (United States)"), the [U.S. 1st Infantry Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1st_Infantry_Division_(United_States) "1st Infantry Division (United States)"), and the [U.S. 1st Armored Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1st_Armored_Division_(United_States) "1st Armored Division (United States)"), a total of 18,500 troops. They were commanded by Major General [Lloyd Fredendall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lloyd_Fredendall "Lloyd Fredendall"), and conveyed from the UK by naval units under Royal Navy Commodore [Thomas Troubridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Hope_Troubridge "Thomas Hope Troubridge").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTERohwer2005209-20) The central task force also included air power from [USS _Ranger_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Ranger_(CV-4) "USS Ranger (CV-4)"), the only true aircraft carrier involved, and the escort carrier [USS _Suwannee_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Suwannee_(CVE-27) "USS Suwannee (CVE-27)") bearing Grumman Wildcats, the US Navy's standard fighter at the time.

Torch was, for propaganda purposes, a landing by U.S. forces, supported by British warships and aircraft, under the belief that this would be more palatable to French public opinion, than an Anglo-American invasion. For the same reason, Churchill suggested that British soldiers might wear [U.S. Army uniforms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uniforms_of_the_United_States_Army "Uniforms of the United States Army"), and [No. 6 Commando](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No._6_Commando "No. 6 Commando") did so.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMangold2012159-21) ([Fleet Air Arm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fleet_Air_Arm "Fleet Air Arm") aircraft did carry [US "star" roundels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_military_aircraft_national_insignia#Roundels "United States military aircraft national insignia") during the operation,[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrown196893-22) and two British destroyers flew the [Stars and Stripes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flag_of_the_United_States "Flag of the United States").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMangold2012159-21)) In reality, the Eastern Task Force, aimed at Algiers, was commanded by [Lieutenant-General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lieutenant-general_(United_Kingdom) "Lieutenant-general (United Kingdom)")[Kenneth Anderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Anderson_(British_Army_officer) "Kenneth Anderson (British Army officer)") and consisted of a brigade from the [British 78th](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/78th_Infantry_Division_(United_Kingdom) "78th Infantry Division (United Kingdom)") and the [U.S. 34th Infantry Divisions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/34th_Infantry_Division_(United_States) "34th Infantry Division (United States)"), along with two British commando units ([No.1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No._1_Commando "No. 1 Commando") and No.6 Commandos), together with the RAF Regiment providing 5 squadrons of infantry and 5 Light anti-aircraft flights, totalling 20,000 troops. During the landing phase, ground forces were to be commanded by U.S. Major General [Charles W. Ryder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_W._Ryder "Charles W. Ryder"), [Commanding General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commanding_officer "Commanding officer") (CG) of the 34th Division and naval forces were commanded by Royal Navy [Vice-Admiral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice-Admiral "Vice-Admiral")[Sir Harold Burrough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Harold_Burrough "Sir Harold Burrough").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTERohwer2005209-20)

Aerial operations were split into two commands, with [Royal Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Air_Force "Royal Air Force") aircraft under [Air Marshal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_Marshal "Air Marshal") Sir [William Welsh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Welsh_(RAF_officer) "William Welsh (RAF officer)") operating east of [Cape Tenez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Tenez "Cape Tenez") in Algeria, and all [United States Army Air Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army_Air_Forces "United States Army Air Forces") aircraft under Major General [Jimmy Doolittle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Doolittle "Jimmy Doolittle"), who was under the direct command of Major General Patton, operating west of Cape Tenez.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPack197844-23)

### Vichy French forces

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Operation_Torch&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Vichy French forces")]

The Vichy French had around 125,000 soldiers in the territories as well as coastal artillery, 210 operational but out-of-date tanks and about 500 aircraft,[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatson200750-24) of which 173 were modern [Dewoitine D.520](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dewoitine_D.520 "Dewoitine D.520") fighters.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTESutherland2011149-25) These forces included 60,000 troops in Morocco, 15,000 in Tunisia, and 50,000 in Algeria.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStamford-26) The bulk of the Vichy French Navy was stationed outside North Africa: three battleships and seven cruisers at [Toulon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toulon "Toulon") and one battleship and three cruisers at Dakar. In North Africa, at Casablanca the incomplete battleship [_Jean Bart_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_battleship_Jean_Bart_(1940) "French battleship Jean Bart (1940)") was used as a coastal battery and there was one cruiser, seven destroyers and eight submarines. At Oran there was a force of four destroyers and nine submarines.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTERohwer2005210-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPack197857-28)

## Battle

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Operation_Torch&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Battle")]

### Eastern task force

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Operation_Torch&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Eastern task force")]

For other battles in the same place, see [Battle of Algiers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Algiers_(disambiguation) "Battle of Algiers (disambiguation)").

[![Image 22: A map showing landings during Operation Torch.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/af/OPERATION-TORCH-OVERVIEW.png/960px-OPERATION-TORCH-OVERVIEW.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:OPERATION-TORCH-OVERVIEW.png "A map showing landings during Operation Torch.")

A map showing landings during Operation Torch.

In the early hours of 8 November, [French Resistance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Resistance "French Resistance") fighters staged a coup in the city of Algiers. They seized control of the city, but when no US troops appeared in the morning, they quickly lost control to Vichy French forces. Meanwhile, the American consul Robert Murphy attempted to persuade General [Alphonse Juin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alphonse_Juin "Alphonse Juin"), the senior French Army officer in North Africa, to side with the Allies and place himself under the command of General Giraud. Murphy learned that Admiral [François Darlan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Darlan "François Darlan"), the commander of all French forces, was also in Algiers on a private visit, and Juin insisted on contacting Darlan at once. Murphy was unable to persuade them to side with the Allies right away, and Darlan contacted Pétain, who instructed him to resist.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacCloskey1971105%E2%80%93106-29)

The invasion commenced with landings on three beaches, two west of Algiers and one east. The landing forces were under the overall command of Major-General Charles W. Ryder, commanding general of the U.S. 34th Infantry Division. The [11th Brigade Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/11th_Infantry_Brigade_and_Headquarters_South_East "11th Infantry Brigade and Headquarters South East") from the British 78th Infantry Division landed on the right-hand beach; the US [168th Regimental Combat Team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/168th_Infantry_Regiment_(United_States) "168th Infantry Regiment (United States)"), from the 34th Infantry Division, supported by 6 Commando and most of 1 Commando, landed on the middle beach; and the US [39th Regimental Combat Team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/39th_Infantry_Regiment_(United_States) "39th Infantry Regiment (United States)"), from the US 9th Infantry Division, supported by the remaining 5 troops from 1 Commando, landed on the left-hand beach. The [36th Brigade Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/36th_Infantry_Brigade_(United_Kingdom) "36th Infantry Brigade (United Kingdom)") from the British 78th Infantry Division stood by in floating reserve.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPlayfairMolonyFlynnGleave2004126,_140%E2%80%9341,_map_18-30) Though some landings went to the wrong beaches, this was immaterial because of the lack of French opposition. Only at [Cape Matifou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bordj_El_Bahri "Bordj El Bahri") a coastal battery opened fire, and in the forenoon some resistance was offered at the fortresses of Cape Matifou, Duperre and L'Empereur. At 06:00 the airfield at [Maison Blanche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houari_Boumediene_Airport "Houari Boumediene Airport") was captured and at 10:00 [Hawker Hurricane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawker_Hurricane "Hawker Hurricane") and [Supermarine Spitfire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supermarine_Spitfire "Supermarine Spitfire") aircraft from [Gibraltar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gibraltar "Gibraltar") started to flow in at the airfield. A second airfield at [Blida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blida_Airport "Blida Airport") surrendered the same day to a British plane landing on the airfield.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPack197863%E2%80%9380-31)

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/33/Near_Algiers%2C_%22Torch%22_troops_hit_the_beaches_behind_a_large_American_flag_%22Left%22_hoping_for_the_French_Army_not_fire..._-_NARA_-_195516.jpg/330px-Near_Algiers%2C_%22Torch%22_troops_hit_the_beaches_behind_a_large_American_flag_%22Left%22_hoping_for_the_French_Army_not_fire..._-_NARA_-_195516.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Near_Algiers,_%22Torch%22_troops_hit_the_beaches_behind_a_large_American_flag_%22Left%22_hoping_for_the_French_Army_not_fire..._-_NARA_-_195516.jpg)

American soldiers land near [Algiers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algiers "Algiers"). The soldier at the dune line is carrying a flag because it was hoped the French would be less likely to fire on Americans.

The only fierce fighting took place in the port of Algiers, where in [Operation Terminal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Terminal "Operation Terminal"), the British destroyers [HMS _Malcolm_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Malcolm_(D19) "HMS Malcolm (D19)") and [HMS _Broke_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Broke_(D83) "HMS Broke (D83)") attempted to land a party of US [Army Rangers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army_Rangers "United States Army Rangers") directly onto the dock, to prevent the French destroying the port facilities and scuttling their ships. Heavy artillery fire hit _Malcolm_ and forced her to abandon the operation, but _Broke_ was able to disembark 250 Rangers who secured the power station and oil installations. At 9:15 however she too had to recall the Rangers and abandon the operation due to the heavy artillery fire. As a result of the damage received, _Broke_ foundered the next day in bad weather.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTERohwer2005209%E2%80%93210-32)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPack197863%E2%80%9380-31)

By 16:00, the US troops had surrounded Algiers and held the coastal batteries defending the harbour. At 18:40 Juin made an agreement with Ryder to stop the fighting. The next day on 9 November a local cease-fire was negotiated and Darlan authorized the Eastern Task Force to use the harbor of Algiers, but in Oran and Morocco the fighting continued. Giraud arrived the same day in Algiers and at noon on 10 November after negotiations with General Clark, Darlan ordered all hostilities to end and to observe neutrality. On secret orders from Pétain, on 11 November he ordered the forces in Tunisia to resist a German invasion.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacCloskey1971106%E2%80%93107-33)

### Western task force

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Operation_Torch&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Western task force")]

The Western Task Force landed before daybreak on 8 November 1942, at three points in Morocco: In the South at [Safi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safi,_Morocco "Safi, Morocco") ([Operation Blackstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Blackstone "Operation Blackstone")), in the North at Mehdiya-[Port Lyautey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenitra "Kenitra") ([Operation Goalpost](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Port_Lyautey "Battle of Port Lyautey")) and the main thrust was at the centre in [Fedala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammedia "Mohammedia"), close to Casablanca, ([Operation Brushwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Brushwood "Operation Brushwood")).[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPack197843-34) Just like in Algiers, there was a failed attempt to neutralize Vichy French command in the morning of 8 November: General [Béthouart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antoine_B%C3%A9thouart "Antoine Béthouart") was unable to convince Admiral [Michelier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frix_Michelier "Frix Michelier") nor General [Noguès](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Nogu%C3%A8s "Charles Noguès") to side with the Allies. Instead they ordered the Army and Navy to oppose the invasion.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBreuer1985110%E2%80%93113-35)

[![Image 24](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cc/Seatrain_Lakehurst_after_discharging_tanks_at_Safi_North_Africa.png/250px-Seatrain_Lakehurst_after_discharging_tanks_at_Safi_North_Africa.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Seatrain_Lakehurst_after_discharging_tanks_at_Safi_North_Africa.png)

[USS _Lakehurst_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Lakehurst_(APV-3/APM-9)#Ship_usage_in_World_War_II_and_Vietnam "USS Lakehurst (APV-3/APM-9)") (formerly _Seatrain New Jersey_), after discharging medium tanks at [Safi, Morocco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safi,_Morocco "Safi, Morocco")

At Safi the objective was to capture the port facilities intact and to land the Western Task Force's medium [Sherman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M4_Sherman "M4 Sherman") tanks, which would be used to reinforce the assault on Casablanca.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHowe199397,_102-36) Two old destroyers, [USS _Cole_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Cole_(DD-155) "USS Cole (DD-155)") and [USS _Bernadou_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Bernadou "USS Bernadou"), were to land an assault party in the harbor, whilst troops landed on the beaches would quickly move to the town. The landings were begun without covering fire, in the hope that the French would not resist at all. However, once French coastal batteries opened fire, Allied warships returned fire. Most of the landings occurred behind schedule, but met no opposition on the beaches. Under cover from fire of the battleship [USS _New York_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_New_York_(BB-34) "USS New York (BB-34)") and cruiser [USS _Philadelphia_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Philadelphia_(CL-41) "USS Philadelphia (CL-41)"), _Cole_ and _Bernadou_ landed their troops and the harbor was captured intact. Safi surrendered on the afternoon of 8 November. By 10 November, the landed troops moved northwards to join the siege of Casablanca.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPack197891%E2%80%9392-37)

At Port-Lyautey, the objective was to secure the port and the airfield, so that aircraft could be flown in from Gibraltar and from aircraft carriers. The landings were delayed because of navigational problems and the slow disembarkation of the troops in their landing ships. The first three waves of troops were landed unopposed on five beaches. The cruiser [USS _Savannah_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Savannah_(CL-42) "USS Savannah (CL-42)") bombarded coastal batteries at [Kasbah Mahdiyya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kasbah_Mahdiyya "Kasbah Mahdiyya"). The next waves came under fire from coastal batteries and Vichy-French aircraft. A first attempt by the old destroyer [USS _Dallas_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Dallas_(DD-199) "USS Dallas (DD-199)") to bring a raiding party inshore on the [Sebou River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sebou_River "Sebou River") to the airfield, failed on 8 November.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPack197892%E2%80%9395-38) Vichy French reinforcements coming from Rabat were bombarded by the battleship [USS _Texas_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Texas_(BB-35) "USS Texas (BB-35)") and the cruiser _Savannah_. A second attempt on 10 November to take the airfield was successful and over the next two days, the escort carrier [USS _Chenango_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Chenango_(CVE-28) "USS Chenango (CVE-28)") sent 77 [Curtiss P-40 Warhawk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curtiss_P-40_Warhawk "Curtiss P-40 Warhawk") to the airfield.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacCloskey1971130-39) With the support of aircraft from the escort carrier [USS _Sangamon_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Sangamon_(CVE-26) "USS Sangamon (CVE-26)"), the Kasbah battery was taken and ships could come closer to shore to unload supplies. On 11 November The cease-fire ordered by Darlan halted all hostilities.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPack197892%E2%80%9395-38)

[![Image 25](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ad/Operation_Torch_-_message_from_the_president_of_United_States_to_the_citizens_of_Casablanca.jpg/250px-Operation_Torch_-_message_from_the_president_of_United_States_to_the_citizens_of_Casablanca.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Operation_Torch_-_message_from_the_president_of_United_States_to_the_citizens_of_Casablanca.jpg)

A flyer in French and Arabic that was distributed by Allied forces in the streets of [Casablanca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casablanca "Casablanca"), calling on citizens to cooperate with the Allied forces

At Fedala, a small port with a large beach 15 miles (24 km) from Casablanca, weather was good but landings were delayed because troopships were not disembarking troops on schedule. The first wave reached shore unopposed at 05:00. Many landing craft were wrecked in the heavy surf or on rocks. At dawn the Vichy French shore batteries opened fire. By 07:30 fire from the cruisers [USS _Augusta_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Augusta_(CA-31) "USS Augusta (CA-31)") and [USS _Brooklyn_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Brooklyn_(CL-40) "USS Brooklyn (CL-40)") with their supporting destroyers, had silenced the shore batteries. At 08:00 when Vichy-French aircraft appeared and attacked, one battery reopened fire. Two Vichy-French destroyers arrived from Casablanca at 08:25 and attacked the American destroyers. By 09:05 the Vichy French destroyers had been driven away, but all available Vichy French ships sortied from Casablanca and at 10:00 renewed the attack on the American ships at Fedala. By 11:00 the battle was over, the two American cruisers had either sunk or driven ashore the light cruiser [_Primauguet_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_cruiser_Primauguet_(1924) "French cruiser Primauguet (1924)"), two flotilla leaders and four destroyers. Only one destroyer escaped back to Casablanca. Fedala surrendered at 14:30 and transport ships could move closer to shore to speed up the unloading.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPack197895%E2%80%9398-40) Meanwhile the American Covering force with the battleship [USS _Massachusetts_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Massachusetts_(BB-59) "USS Massachusetts (BB-59)") had appeared before Casablanca and when coastal batteries opened fire at 07:00, the American ships responded at once and damaged the Vichy-French battleship _Jean Bart_ with five hits, putting its one operational turret out of action.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacCloskey1971122-41) Of the eleven submarines in port, three were destroyed but the other eight took up attack positions. These submarines attacked _Massachusetts_; the aircraft carrier [USS _Ranger_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Ranger_(CV-4) "USS Ranger (CV-4)"); and the cruisers _Brooklyn_ and [_Tuscaloosa_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Tuscaloosa_(CA-37) "USS Tuscaloosa (CA-37)"), but all their torpedoes missed, and six submarines were sunk.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTERohwer2005210-27)

On 9 November the small port of Fedala was in use and troops advanced on Casablanca. Despite having lost 55 aircraft the previous day, attacks by Vichy-French aircraft continued all day.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPack197895%E2%80%9398-40) On 10 November, _Jean Bart_ was repaired, but when she opened fire, she was attacked by dive-bombers from the aircraft carrier _Ranger_ and heavily damaged by two bomb hits.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorison1947162%E2%80%93163-42) The Americans surrounded the port of Casablanca by 10 November but waited for the arrival of the tanks from Safi to start an all-out attack planned for 11 November at 07:15. Orders from Darlan, broadcast on 10 November, to cease resistance were ignored until 11 November 06:00, the city surrendered an hour before the final assault was due to take place.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPack197895%E2%80%9398-40)

### Center task force

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Operation_Torch&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Center task force")]

[![Image 26](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b3/The_Royal_Navy_during_the_Second_World_War-_Operation_Torch%2C_North_Africa%2C_November_1942_A12667.jpg/250px-The_Royal_Navy_during_the_Second_World_War-_Operation_Torch%2C_North_Africa%2C_November_1942_A12667.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Royal_Navy_during_the_Second_World_War-_Operation_Torch,_North_Africa,_November_1942_A12667.jpg)

U.S. troops landing in Arzew, with troopships in the background

The Center Task Force was split among three beaches, two west of Oran and one east. Landings at the westernmost beach were delayed because of a French convoy which appeared while the minesweepers were clearing a path. Some delay and confusion, and damage to landing ships, was caused by the unexpected shallowness of water and sandbars. On all beaches the landings met no resistance.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPack197881%E2%80%9390-43)

An airborne assault by the 2nd Battalion, 509th Parachute Infantry Regiment, which flew all the way from England, over Spain, to Oran, to capture the airfields at [Tafraoui](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tafraoui "Tafraoui") and [La Sénia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Es_S%C3%A9nia "Es Sénia") failed.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPlayfairMolonyFlynnGleave2004146%E2%80%9347,_map_19-44)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPack197881%E2%80%9390-43) The operation was marked by communicational and navigational problems owing to the anti-aircraft and beacon ship HMS _Alynbank_ broadcasting on the wrong frequency.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-:0-45) Poor weather over Spain and the extreme range caused the formation to scatter and forced 30 of the 37 air transports to land in the dry salt lake to the west of the objective.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPlayfairMolony149-46) Of the other aircraft, one pilot became disoriented and landed his plane in [Gibraltar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gibraltar "Gibraltar"). Two others landed in [French Morocco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_protectorate_in_Morocco "French protectorate in Morocco") and three in [Spanish Morocco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_protectorate_in_Morocco "Spanish protectorate in Morocco"), where another Dakota dropped its paratroopers by mistake. A total of 67 American troops were interned by [Franco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francisco_Franco "Francisco Franco")'s forces until February 1943. Tafraoui and La Sénia were eventually captured but the role played by the airborne forces in Operation Torch was minimal.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-:0-45) Aircraft from three British carriers attacked these airfields in the morning and destroyed seventy airplanes which were armed and ready to take off to attack. In the afternoon the Tafraoui airfield was captured by the quickly advancing troops from the beachheads, and immediately Spitfires were flown in from Gibraltar. The [U.S. 1st Ranger Battalion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1st_Ranger_Battalion_(United_States) "1st Ranger Battalion (United States)") landed east of Oran and quickly captured the shore battery at [Arzew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arzew "Arzew").[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPack197881%E2%80%9390-43)

At the same time of the landings, in the early morning of 8 November, an [attempt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Reservist "Operation Reservist") was made to land U.S. infantry by the sloops [HMS _Walney_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USCGC_Sebago_(1930) "USCGC Sebago (1930)") and [HMS _Hartland_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USCGC_Pontchartrain_(1928) "USCGC Pontchartrain (1928)") at the harbor of Oran, in order to prevent destruction of the port facilities and scuttling of ships. But both sloops were sunk by Vichy-French destroyers in the harbour and the operation failed.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPack197881%E2%80%9390-43) The Vichy French naval fleet consisting of one flotilla leader, three destroyers, one minesweeper, six submarines and some smaller vessels, broke out from the harbor and attacked the Allied invasion fleet. Over the next two days all these ships were either sunk or driven ashore, only one submarine escaped to Toulon, after an unsuccessful attack on the cruiser [HMS _Jamaica_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Jamaica_(44) "HMS Jamaica (44)").[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTERohwer2005209%E2%80%93210-32) French batteries and the invasion fleet exchanged fire throughout 8–9 November, with French troops defending Oran and the surrounding area stubbornly; bombardment by the British battleship [HMS _Rodney_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Rodney_(29) "HMS Rodney (29)") brought about Oran's surrender on 10 November.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPack197881%E2%80%9390-43)

### Axis reaction

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Operation_Torch&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Axis reaction")]

In the central and eastern Atlantic, U-boats had been drawn away to attack trade [convoy SL 125](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convoy_SL_125 "Convoy SL 125"),[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwards1999115-47) and troop convoys between the UK and North Africa went largely unnoticed. A [Focke-Wulf Fw 200 Condor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Focke-Wulf_Fw_200_Condor "Focke-Wulf Fw 200 Condor") detected on 31 October a task force of aircraft carriers and cruisers, and on 2 November a returning [U-boat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U-boat "U-boat") reported a troop ship convoy.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlair199888%E2%80%9389-48)

On 4 November the Germans became aware of an impending big operation, they anticipated another convoy run to Malta or an amphibious landing in Libya or at [Bougie Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C3%A9ja%C3%AFa "Béjaïa"). Seven U-boats of the Atlantic force were ordered to break through the [Strait of Gibraltar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strait_of_Gibraltar "Strait of Gibraltar") and go to the North African coast. Nine Mediterranean U-boats were also deployed to the same region.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlair199889%E2%80%9397-49) A total of nineteen U-boats were stationed between the [Balearic Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balearic_Islands "Balearic Islands") and Algiers, whilst the Italian Navy deployed twenty-one submarines East of Algiers.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTERohwer2005208%E2%80%93209-50) On 7 November five German submarines made contact with the British invasion forces but all their attacks missed their target. On 8 November most of these U-boats were operating near Bougie and missed the landings at Algiers.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlair199889%E2%80%9397-49) When receiving news of the landings, [Dönitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_D%C3%B6nitz "Karl Dönitz") ordered twenty-five of the Atlantic U-boats to move towards the Morocco area and Gibraltar, leaving only ten U-boats in the North Atlantic and bringing the U-boat [main offensive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Atlantic "Battle of the Atlantic") against the convoy lanes to the United Kingdom to a virtual standstill.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlair1998107-51) The first wave of nine U-boats to arrive off Morocco ran into a well-prepared defense and achieved little. Only [_U-130_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_submarine_U-130_(1941) "German submarine U-130 (1941)") sank three large transports on the anchorage of Fedala, forcing the port to close and ships to divert to Casablanca.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlair1998110-52) The second wave of fourteen U-boats was sent to the area West of Gibraltar, trying to block all traffic in and out the Straits. They sank the escort carrier [HMS _Avenger_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Avenger_(D14) "HMS Avenger (D14)") and the destroyer tender [HMS _Hecla_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Hecla_(1940) "HMS Hecla (1940)") with heavy loss of life. In both theaters of operation, the Mediterranean and Atlantic, the Germans lost eight U-boats,[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlair1998111%E2%80%93115-53) and the Italians two.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTERohwer2005209-20) Between 8 and 14 November German bomber and torpedo aircraft attacked ships along the North African coast. They sank two troop transports, one landing ship, two transport ships and the sloop [_Ibis_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Ibis "HMS Ibis"). The aircraft carrier [_Argus_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Argus_(I49) "HMS Argus (I49)") and the monitor [_Roberts_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Roberts_(F40) "HMS Roberts (F40)") were damaged by bombs.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTERohwer2005210-27)

### Assault on Bougie

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Operation_Torch&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Assault on Bougie")]

[![Image 27](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/52/North_Africa_Operations._12_November_1942%2C_Bougie%2C_North_Africa._A13019.jpg/250px-North_Africa_Operations._12_November_1942%2C_Bougie%2C_North_Africa._A13019.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:North_Africa_Operations._12_November_1942,_Bougie,_North_Africa._A13019.jpg)

_Karanja_ and [_Cathay_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SS_Cathay_(1924) "SS Cathay (1924)") on fire off Bougie after Axis air attacks

There were limited land communications to move quickly from Algiers eastwards to Tunisia. The Allies had planned additional landings at Bougie and Bone in order to speed up that advance, but there were not enough resources available to execute these landings together with the main landings at Oran and Algiers. On 10 November the British 36th Infantry Brigade was boarded on three troop transports which landed unopposed, under the cover of a bombardment force in the harbor of Bougie on 11 November. A further troop transport was to land commandos, RAF personnel and petrol at [Djidelli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jijel "Jijel"), with the goal to capture the airfield there and provide air cover over Bougie. Due to the heavy surf, this landing was delayed and finally diverted to Bougie and as a consequence air cover was only available from 13 November onward. The Axis air force based in Sardinia and Sicily exploited the lack of air cover between 11 and 13 November to execute heavy attacks on the harbour of Bougie.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPack197899%E2%80%93104-54) They sank the empty troop transports [_Cathay_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SS_Cathay_(1924) "SS Cathay (1924)"), [_Awatea_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMT_Awatea "HMT Awatea") and the landing ship _Karanja_.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTERohwer2005210-27)

## Aftermath

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Operation_Torch&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Aftermath")]

### Political results

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Operation_Torch&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Political results")]

Main articles: [François Darlan §Darlan's deal in North Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Darlan#Darlan's_deal_in_North_Africa "François Darlan"), and [French Civil and Military High Command](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Civil_and_Military_High_Command "French Civil and Military High Command")

It quickly became clear that Giraud lacked the authority to take command of the French forces. He preferred to wait in Gibraltar for the results of the landing. However, Darlan in Algiers had such authority. Eisenhower, with the support of Roosevelt and Churchill, made an [agreement with Darlan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clark-Darlan_accords "Clark-Darlan accords"), recognising him as French "High Commissioner" in North Africa. In return, Darlan ordered all French forces in North Africa to cease resistance to the Allies and to cooperate instead. The deal was made on 10 November, and French resistance ceased almost at once. The French troops in North Africa who were not already captured submitted to and eventually joined the Allied forces.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEisenhower194899%E2%80%93105,_107%E2%80%9310-55) Men from French North Africa would see much combat under the Allied banner as part of the [French Expeditionary Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Expeditionary_Corps_(1943%E2%80%9344) "French Expeditionary Corps (1943–44)") (consisting of 112,000 troops in April 1944) in the [Italian campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_Campaign_(World_War_II) "Italian Campaign (World War II)"), where Maghrebis (mostly Moroccans) made up over 60% of the unit's soldiers.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGaujac200331-56)

When [Adolf Hitler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolf_Hitler "Adolf Hitler") learned of Darlan's deal with the Allies, he immediately ordered [the occupation of Vichy France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Case_Anton "Case Anton").[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTESatloff-57)

The Eisenhower/Darlan agreement meant that the officials appointed by the Vichy regime would remain in power in North Africa. No role was provided for Free France, which deeply offended De Gaulle. It also offended much of the British and American public, who regarded all Vichy French as Nazi collaborators. Eisenhower insisted that he had no real choice if his forces were to move on against the Axis in Tunisia, rather than fight the French in Algeria and Morocco.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGelb1992255%E2%80%93264-58) On 24 December, [Fernand Bonnier de La Chapelle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernand_Bonnier_de_La_Chapelle "Fernand Bonnier de La Chapelle"), a French resistance fighter and anti-fascist monarchist, assassinated Darlan. Giraud succeeded Darlan but, like him, replaced few of the Vichy officials. Under pressure from the Allies and De Gaulle's supporters, the French régime shifted, with Vichy officials gradually replaced and its more offensive decrees rescinded.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGelb1992272%E2%80%93282-59)

### Military consequences

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Operation_Torch&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Military consequences")]

#### Toulon

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Operation_Torch&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Toulon")]

Main article: [Scuttling of the French fleet in Toulon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scuttling_of_the_French_fleet_in_Toulon "Scuttling of the French fleet in Toulon")

Darlan ordered cease fire in North Africa on 10 November, and the next day the Germans and the Italians invaded Vichy France. One of their goals was to seize the French fleet in Toulon. Darlan invited the French commander of the fleet in Toulon, [Jean de Laborde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_de_Laborde "Jean de Laborde") to join the Allies, but instead the French commander ordered the fleet scuttled on 27 November when the Germans entered Toulon.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPack1978106%E2%80%93107-60)

[![Image 29](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8e/Axis_prisoners_of_war_are_herded_out_of_the_city_as_Allied_armies_enter_Tunis._-_NARA_-_195472.jpg/250px-Axis_prisoners_of_war_are_herded_out_of_the_city_as_Allied_armies_enter_Tunis._-_NARA_-_195472.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Axis_prisoners_of_war_are_herded_out_of_the_city_as_Allied_armies_enter_Tunis._-_NARA_-_195472.jpg)

Italian prisoners of war in Tunisia

#### Tunisia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Operation_Torch&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Tunisia")]

Main articles: [Tunisia Campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tunisia_Campaign "Tunisia Campaign") and [Run for Tunis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Run_for_Tunis "Run for Tunis")

After the German and Italian occupation of Vichy France, the French _[Armée d'Afrique](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Army\_of\_Africa\_(France) "Army of Africa (France)")_ sided with the Allies, providing a third corps ([XIX Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/XIX_Army_Corps_(France) "XIX Army Corps (France)")) for the [First Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Army_(United_Kingdom) "First Army (United Kingdom)") under the command of Anderson.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGelb1992298-61) On 9 November, Axis forces started to build up in French Tunisia, unopposed by the local French forces.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatson200760-62) After consolidating in Algeria, the Allies began the [Tunisia Campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tunisia_Campaign "Tunisia Campaign"). Elements of the First Army came to within 40 mi (64 km) of [Tunis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tunis "Tunis") before a [counterattack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counterattack "Counterattack") at [Djedeida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Djedeida "Djedeida") thrust them back.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacCloskey1971141%E2%80%93142-63) Meanwhile, after their victory at El-Alamein, the [Eighth Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eighth_Army_(United_Kingdom) "Eighth Army (United Kingdom)") under Lieutenant-General [Bernard Montgomery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_Montgomery "Bernard Montgomery") was pushing German and Italian troops under _[Generalfeldmarschall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generalfeldmarschall "Generalfeldmarschall")_ Erwin Rommel steadily towards Tunisia from the East. In January 1943 they reached South Tunisia where Axis troops made a stand at the [Mareth Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mareth_Line "Mareth Line").[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorison1947258-64) In the west, the [US II Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/II_Corps_(United_States) "II Corps (United States)") suffered defeats at the [Battle of Sidi Bou Zid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Sidi_Bou_Zid "Battle of Sidi Bou Zid") on 14–15 February and the [Battle of Kasserine Pass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Kasserine_Pass "Battle of Kasserine Pass") on 19 February, but Allied reinforcements halted the Axis advance on 22 February. Fredendall was sacked and replaced by [George Patton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Patton "George Patton").[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGelb1992209-65)[General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_(United_Kingdom) "General (United Kingdom)") Sir [Harold Alexander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harold_Alexander,_1st_Earl_Alexander_of_Tunis "Harold Alexander, 1st Earl Alexander of Tunis") arrived in Tunisia in late February as commander of the new [18th Army Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/18th_Army_Group "18th Army Group"), which had been created to command the Eighth Army and the Allied forces fighting in Tunisia. The Axis forces attacked eastward at the [Battle of Medenine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Medenine "Battle of Medenine") on 6 March but were easily repulsed by the Eighth Army. On 9 March, Rommel left Tunisia to be replaced by [Jürgen von Arnim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J%C3%BCrgen_von_Arnim "Jürgen von Arnim").[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGelb1992299%E2%80%93311-66) The First and Eighth Armies [attacked](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Vulcan "Operation Vulcan") again in April. On 6 May the British took Tunis and American forces reached [Bizerte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bizerte "Bizerte") on 7 May. By 13 May, all Axis forces in Tunisia had surrendered.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorison1947259%E2%80%93260-67)

## Later influence

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Operation_Torch&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Later influence")]

Despite Operation Torch's role in the war and logistical success, it has been largely overlooked in many popular histories of the war and in general cultural influence. _[The Economist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Economist "The Economist")_ speculated that this was because French forces were the initial enemies of the landing, making for a difficult fit into the war's overall narrative in general histories. The operation was America's first armed deployment in the [Arab world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab_world "Arab world") since the [Barbary Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbary_Wars "Barbary Wars") and, according to _The Economist_, laid the foundations for America's postwar [Middle East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_East "Middle East") policy.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEconomist-68)

Allied landing operations in French North Africa during World War II

This article is about the World War II Allied campaign in North Africa. For Biafran offensive during the Nigerian Civil War, see [Midwest Invasion of 1967](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midwest_Invasion_of_1967 "Midwest Invasion of 1967").
